The Supreme Court examined whether the Registrar of Cooperative Societies could refuse leave to continue a suit under Section 112 of the Gujarat Co-operative Societies Act, 1961, on the ground that it failed to comply with the notice requirement under Section 167. The Court held that determining the tenability of a suit is a judicial function exclusively within the competence of civil courts, and thus the Registrar's refusal was without jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, holding that a conditional Essentiality Certificate submitted for establishing a new medical college does not comply with the mandatory requirements under MCI regulations. The Court ruled that the High Court was not justified in directing consideration of a fresh certificate after the statutory deadline, as conditional certificates cannot substitute for unconditional ones. Consequently, the lower courts' orders were set aside and the Trust was directed to submit a fresh application for the next academic year in compliance with prescribed time schedules.

The appellant challenged the High Court's direction to execute a patent transfer deed based on an initial draft following a Partial Final Arbitral Award. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned order, holding that the appellant had duly complied with the award by executing the deed as per the respondent's subsequent re-draft, and found the appellant not liable for the respondent's misfeasance in refusing to accept it.

The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's suo motu order that scrutinized and stayed a provision of the Meghalaya Lokayukta Act, 2014, ruling that courts cannot test the constitutional validity of statutory provisions or grant stays in suo motu PILs. Emphasizing judicial restraint, the Court held that while suo motu PILs are permissible for rare public interest matters, they cannot be used to challenge specific legislative provisions under Article 226, and directed the executive to establish the Lokayukta institution.

The Supreme Court allowed an appeal against a High Court order that had set aside the attachment of a flat belonging to a judgment-debtor. The Court found that the mother and daughter collusively executed sham documents after a compensation order attained finality solely to delay execution and defeat the decree-holder's recovery. Consequently, the attachment was restored as the documents were fabricated to frustrate lawful execution proceedings.

The Supreme Court dismissed appeals filed by the Delhi Development Authority, holding that land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, lapse under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, if physical possession was not taken or compensation paid within five years prior to the 2013 Act's commencement. The Court further clarified that merely passing an award under Section 11 of the 1894 Act does not automatically vest the land in the Government; actual possession by the Collector is required for vesting.

In a multi-accused case under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, the Supreme Court held that when one accused exercises the right to re-analyze a food sample under Section 13(2), the resulting Central Food Laboratory certificate supersedes the Public Analyst's report for all co-accused. Consequently, the Court set aside the High Court's order and quashed the criminal proceedings, ruling that statutory re-analysis benefits extend to all co-accused rather than solely the applicant.

The Supreme Court allowed appeals by landowners seeking release of acquired land under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, holding that symbolic possession is insufficient to trigger vesting under Section 16 and that the land likely falls within the village's 'Lal Dora'. The Court remanded the matter to the High Powered Committee to verify the Lal Dora status and directed that the appellants receive similar treatment as neighboring properties, prohibiting denial of release solely based on Section 16 vesting.

This case concerns appeals against penalties imposed by SEBI for alleged technical violations of insider trading regulations. The central legal issue is the interplay between Sections 15A and 15J of the SEBI Act, 1992, particularly whether the expression 'namely' in Section 15J exhaustively limits an adjudicating officer's discretion in determining penalty quantum, and how the 2002 and 2014 legislative amendments affected this discretion. Finding irreconcilable contradictions in prior precedents and potential unreasonableness in strict statutory application, the Court referred the matter to a larger Bench for authoritative clarification.

The appellants were convicted for unlawful assembly, rioting, abduction, and voluntarily causing hurt after allegedly attacking and abducting a victim whose body was never recovered. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the lower courts' findings that an independent injured witness corroborated the family witnesses and that the appellants consistently shared a common object to commit the offences.

The Supreme Court examined a challenge to the Government's policy on allocating additional Colonel vacancies in the Indian Army between operational units and service/support corps. Upholding the 'Command Exit Model' allocation as valid and non-discriminatory, the Court set aside the Armed Forces Tribunal's order, emphasized the limited scope of judicial review in military policy, and directed the creation of 141 additional posts for the Combat Support stream to rectify prior allocation errors.

The Supreme Court addressed the critical need to protect Good Samaritans from police harassment and legal liability when they assist road accident victims. The Court approved and modified the Government's Good Samaritan Guidelines, granting them the force of law under Articles 32, 142, and 141 of the Constitution until proper legislation is enacted, while directing police and courts to treat affidavits as complete statements and avoid detaining helpers.

The Supreme Court allowed the State's criminal appeal against the High Court's acquittal of a doctor accused of murdering his pregnant wife by forcibly administering poison. Examining medical evidence of struggle injuries, the accused's failure to explain circumstances, evidence of poison purchase, and delayed hospitalization, the Court held that the chain of circumstances unerringly pointed to guilt. The plea for sentencing leniency based on a surviving minor child was rejected due to the heinous nature of the offence, and the trial court's conviction was restored.

The case centered on whether a Metropolitan Magistrate has jurisdiction to grant tender of pardon to an approver under Section 306 of the CrPC in a case triable by a Special Judge under the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, holding that the Magistrate is specifically empowered to grant such pardon prior to committal, and that any procedural irregularity would not vitiate the trial under Section 460 of the CrPC.

topics: Jurisdiction of Magistrate vs. Special Judge

query: The Supreme Court examined whether the Court of Session is empowered to take cognizance of an offence when the committing Magistrate had previously rejected a similar application to charge additional accused. The Court held that upon committal under Section 193 CrPC, the Sessions Court acts as a Court of original jurisdiction and takes cognizance for the first time, rendering the Magistrate's prior refusal non-preclusive. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, upholding the Sessions Court's order.

The State appealed against the trial court's acquittal of a public official charged with demanding and accepting illegal gratification under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The Supreme Court upheld the acquittal, holding that mere recovery of money without proof of demand does not trigger the statutory presumption under Section 20, and appellate courts should not interfere with a trial court's acquittal unless the findings are perverse or legally unsustainable.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's order, ruling that a landlord cannot evict a tenant-company undergoing liquidation for non-payment of rent without issuing the mandatory statutory notice under Section 12 of the Bombay Rent Act. The Court held that the tenant's readiness and willingness to pay rent preserves statutory protection, and since a company in liquidation retains its corporate existence until formally dissolved, the Official Liquidator cannot be automatically directed to hand over possession of the leased property to the landlord.

The Supreme Court allowed the criminal appeal and set aside the High Court's order quashing the criminal complaint against the respondent for smuggling gold biscuits via an aircraft. The Court held that exoneration in customs adjudication proceedings does not amount to a binding acquittal in a criminal trial, and given the respondent's evasion of investigation and admissible co-accused statements, the criminal proceedings were rightly continued.

The State appealed against the High Court's acquittal of the deceased's father-in-law, mother-in-law, and brother-in-law in a dowry death case. The Supreme Court upheld the acquittal, holding that monetary demands were customary gifts, a Rs. 20,000 demand was too remote to satisfy the 'soon before death' requirement under Section 304B IPC, and no overt acts of cruelty were established against the co-accused.

The Supreme Court dismissed the State of Maharashtra's appeals against the High Court's acquittal of the accused in a murder case, ruling that the prosecution failed to establish their identity beyond reasonable doubt. The Court found critical inconsistencies in eyewitness accounts, procedural defects, and undue delays in conducting the Test Identification Parades, which justified granting the benefit of doubt to the accused.

The Supreme Court examined whether a Trial Court's subsequent decision to take cognizance of offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, after initially directing the filing of sanction orders, amounted to an impermissible review under Section 362 of the CrPC. The Court held that the initial direction was merely a deferral and not a final order, thus allowing the Trial Court to take cognizance upon learning no sanction was required. The appeal was allowed and the matter remitted to the High Court to determine afresh whether prior sanction was necessary.

The Supreme Court allowed the criminal appeal, overturning the appellant's murder conviction under Section 302 of the IPC and substituting it with culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I. The Court found no premeditated motive, holding that the fatal assault resulted from a minor dispute and sudden provocation following a juvenile co-accused's cries. The life imprisonment sentence was reduced to the over 12 years already undergone, and the appellant was directed to be released.

The Supreme Court set aside the conviction of the appellant under Sections 302/34 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code, holding that the prosecution failed to complete the chain of circumstantial evidence. The Court found the last seen theory legally unsustainable due to a seven-day time gap between the deceased being last seen alive and the recovery of skeletal remains, and noted an unexplained delay in filing the complaint. Additionally, the prosecution could not establish that the recovered bones belonged to the deceased or that the death resulted from homicide, and the deceased's wife's court testimony contained material improvements that undermined its reliability.

The Supreme Court examined whether a court adjudicating a complaint under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 possesses the jurisdiction to allow amendments to the original petition. The Court held that proceedings under Sections 18 and 20 are predominantly civil in nature, granting courts the power to permit amendments to avoid multiplicity of litigation and advance substantive justice. The criminal appeal was consequently dismissed.

The Court examined whether criminal proceedings under the Insecticide Act, 1968 could continue after the statutory 28-day period for challenging an analyst's report had expired. It held that this limitation applies only to the person from whom the sample was seized, and since the appellants lost the vital right to re-test the sample through no fault of their own, the proceedings were quashed.

The case examined whether Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 applies to a foreign award when parties explicitly choose a foreign seat and governing law. The Supreme Court ruled that such a choice expressly excludes Part I of the Act, barring Indian courts from entertaining setting-aside proceedings under Section 34. Consequently, the Court upheld the High Court's order enforcing the foreign award under Part II of the Act.

The Supreme Court examined whether the mandatory prior approval for taking cognizance under Section 20A of the TADA Act could be granted by an officer higher in rank than the designated District Superintendent of Police. Holding that statutory powers vested in a specifically named authority cannot be exercised by superiors, the Court ruled the approval was invalid, thereby vitiating the trial. Consequently, the appeals by the convicted accused were allowed, setting aside their convictions and ordering their immediate release, while the State's appeals were dismissed.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, holding that judicial interference is impermissible once an election process has commenced, particularly when an alternative statutory remedy exists. The Court ruled that election disputes must be resolved after the election is completed, directing the respondent to approach the Central Government under Section 5 of the Dentists Act, 1948.

The appeal concerned a dispute over possession of a property involving a widow's estate, reversionary rights, and the validity of a sale deed executed by the deceased widow's sister. The Court held that the respondent's claim of adoption was not established, the sister was the lawful heir, and the sale deed was valid, entitling the appellant to possession based on title. The High Court's judgment dismissing the suit was set aside, and the first appellate court's decree was restored.

The Supreme Court allowed an appeal concerning a suit for specific performance of a property agreement, resolving a dispute over whether 'built-up area' includes common spaces like corridors and lobbies. The Court held that since the defendant had explicitly agreed to the plaintiff's definition excluding common areas, the defendant could not subsequently resile from that mutually accepted position under Section 5 of the Indian Contract Act. Consequently, the High Court's decision was set aside and the trial court's decree was restored.

The appellant, who was transferred to Pondicherry and terminated due to unit closure, filed a complaint in the Labour Court at Aurangabad, where he was originally employed and where the management took the closure decision. The Supreme Court held that because the termination decision was made in Aurangabad, a cause of action arose there, granting the Aurangabad Labour Court concurrent jurisdiction alongside the Pondicherry Labour Court. The appeal is allowed, the High Court's order is set aside, and the case is remanded to the Aurangabad Labour Court for consideration on merits.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's order acquitting twelve accused persons convicted of murder and conspiracy. The Court found material alterations in eye-witness statements, failure to identify the assailants, unestablished recovery of weapons, and a lack of cogent evidence to prove the alleged conspiracy. Consequently, the Court held there were no compelling reasons to interfere with the acquittal.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and upheld the resumption of a 6-acre land allotted to the respondent, finding that the respondent concealed material facts regarding the transfer of shares and assets in violation of Rule 9 of the Chandigarh Information Services Park Rules, 2002 and Clause 15 of the allotment letter. The Court held that the respondent did not come with clean hands after failing to disclose these transactions despite a clear judicial direction, thereby rendering the High Court's order setting aside the resumption unsustainable.

The Supreme Court examined the High Court's refusal to grant leave to appeal against an order of acquittal in a murder case. The Court held that the High Court's failure to record reasons for denying leave amounted to non-application of mind and violated established legal principles. Accordingly, the appeal was allowed, the impugned order was set aside, and the matter was remanded to the High Court for fresh consideration on merits.

The Supreme Court upheld the Government's policy allowing the migration of Broadband Wireless Access (BWA) spectrum licenses to Unified Licenses (UL) and the fixation of migration fees and Spectrum Usage Charges. The Court ruled that judicial review of economic and policy decisions must be minimal and non-interfering, provided the policy stems from expert deliberations and is not arbitrary or unlawful. Consequently, the writ petition was dismissed, affirming that no undue advantage was granted and no wrongful loss was caused to the public exchequer.

The Supreme Court examined whether the High Court, exercising first appellate jurisdiction under Section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, discharged its statutory duty to appreciate evidence and decide all issues on facts and law. The Court held that such appeals require comprehensive adjudication akin to Section 96 of the CPC and found the High Court's cryptic judgment legally unsustainable for failing to record reasoned findings. Consequently, the appeal was partly allowed and the matter was remanded to the High Court for a fresh decision on merits.

The Supreme Court allowed the criminal appeal and restored the magistrate's order discharging the accused, holding that continuing prosecution after an administrative tribunal has exonerated them on merits amounts to an abuse of process. The Court clarified that since the Revenue did not challenge the tribunal's final order, the High Court lacked jurisdiction to re-examine the merits of the case.

The appellant challenged the denial of back wages after being reinstated following a resignation forced under compulsion and criminal intimidation. The Court held that payment of back wages is discretionary and requires proof of unemployment during the disputed period. Consequently, back wages were denied, but the appellant was awarded Rs. 25,000 for wrongful denial of service and directed to be reinstated with consequential benefits.

The Supreme Court examined whether land acquisition proceedings initiated under the 1894 Act lapsed under Section 24 of the 2013 Act when no award was passed. The Court held that since no award was made, there is no statutory lapse, but directed the authority to pass the award and determine compensation under the 2013 Act within six months. The High Court's order quashing the acquisition was set aside.

The Supreme Court held that land acquisition proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 lapse under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act if compensation has not been paid to the landowner or deposited in court. The Court ruled that the statutory duty to pay compensation lies with the Requisitioning Authority, not the landowner, and accordingly allowed the appeal, setting aside the acquisition proceedings.

Private tour operators filed writ petitions under Article 32 seeking directions for registration to conduct Haj tours, apprehending arbitrary rejection by authorities. The Court accepted the government's undertaking that no decisions had yet been made and granted liberty to file fresh applications, directing concerned authorities to evaluate each on its merits and pass reasoned orders in accordance with law. The writ petitions were disposed of accordingly.

The Supreme Court allowed the civil appeal, holding the respondents negligent for failing to maintain a safe water level in the dam before the monsoon, thereby rejecting the 'act of God' defence. Relying on the doctrine of strict liability, the Court found the respondents liable for flooding the appellants' agricultural land and destroying their fruit trees. Exercising powers under Article 142 of the Constitution, the Court awarded Rs. 5,00,000 as reasonable compensation, noting that the wrongdoer bears the risk of inaccurate damage quantification.

The Supreme Court held that inter-state sales of goods manufactured by an exempted industrial unit are exempt from tax under Section 8(5) of the Central Sales Tax Act, regardless of whether the sale is made by the manufacturer or a third-party dealer. The Court clarified that the exemption pertains to the goods themselves rather than being restricted to the first sale, and that the notification's proviso merely requires the manufacturer to have not charged tax initially.

The appeal concerns whether a notice of arbitration was barred by limitation, specifically examining when the cause of action arises in a work contract. The Supreme Court held that the cause of action accrues when a real dispute emerges through assertion and denial of a right, rather than merely upon contract completion. Consequently, the arbitration notice was within the limitation period, the High Court's order was upheld, and the civil appeal is dismissed.

The Supreme Court examined whether an arbitrator under the Arbitration Act, 1940 retains the power to award pendente lite interest when the underlying contract contains a bar. The Court held that an arbitrator cannot award such interest if expressly barred by the agreement, but a mere restriction on interest for delayed payment does not automatically constitute an express ouster of this power, and the determination must depend on the overall intention of the contract.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the appellant cooperative society cannot challenge the mandatory open auction process or the highest bid amount for a ghat settlement after having accepted the contract under protest. The Court emphasized that the auction was conducted transparently pursuant to government circulars to augment state revenue, and ruled that the appellant's prior acceptance estops it from later contesting the bid as arbitrary or unreasonable.

The case concerns a dispute over state government recruitment where a change in reservation policy led to a High Court direction to either create shadow posts or push down reserved-category appointees, which the State implemented without hearing the affected officers. The Supreme Court held that after 25 years of uninterrupted service, the appellants' continuance in their posts would not prejudice anyone and should not be disturbed, thereby disposing of the appeal without altering their existing appointments.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, upholding the State Government's right to verify disability certificates issued by the Medical Board following complaints of widespread fraud in reserved category recruitments. Relying on the settled principle that fraud vitiates all solemn acts, the Court held that the High Court erred by restricting verification to physical checks, which could perpetuate the fraud. Consequently, the impugned High Court order was set aside and the writ petition dismissed.

The Supreme Court dismissed the criminal appeal against the appellant's conviction for murdering his father under Section 302 IPC. The Court upheld the lower courts' findings, relying on corroborated eyewitness testimony, forensic evidence matching the victim's blood group to the appellant's clothes, and the appellant's failure to explain the homicidal death when found alone with the deceased, while accepting the prosecution's explanation for the delay in registering the FIR.

The petitioner, a physically handicapped Scheduled Caste officer, challenged his non-selection for the Indian Administrative Service, claiming entitlement to a 3% disability reservation under Section 33 of the PWD Act, 1995. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on grounds entirely distinct from the Tribunal's ruling, prompting the Supreme Court to grant special leave and tag the appeal with other pending civil appeals concerning disability reservation and service selection regulations for a comprehensive determination.

The Supreme Court examined whether the appellant's conviction for attempt to murder under Section 307 IPC was sustainable given ambiguous medical evidence regarding grievous versus simple injuries. The Court converted the conviction to voluntarily causing hurt under Section 324 IPC and granted the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act, ordering the appellant's release on executing a bond due to the prolonged delay and his settled personal circumstances.

The Supreme Court's five-judge bench allowed review petitions against its 2013 judgment in the Christian Medical College case, recalling the original decision and directing a fresh hearing. The bench held that the original judgment failed to consider binding precedents and lacked proper discussion among its members, and declined to provide detailed reasons to avoid prejudicing the re-hearing.

The Supreme Court examined whether a bank could claim 50% of the increase in the fair market value of a mortgaged property when the borrower entered into an agreement to sell within a three-year One Time Settlement (OTS) lock-in period. The Court held that an agreement to sell does not constitute an actual sale under the OTS terms, and since no sale occurred within the restricted period, the bank was not entitled to a share of the increased value. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed, directing the bank to accept the OTS payment and release the property title and possession to the respondent.

The Supreme Court dismissed an appeal challenging the High Court's affirmation of a Magistrate's order to summon two officials under Section 319 CrPC for embezzling MNREGA funds. The Court held that an FIR is not an exhaustive record of all facts or accused, and the police's failure to charge a suspect does not strip the trial court of its statutory power to summon additional accused based on evidence recorded during trial.

The Supreme Court upheld its prior order directing the demolition of an unauthorized multi-storeyed building that significantly deviated from sanctioned building plans and Floor Area Ratio limits. Rejecting proposals to compound the illegal construction, the Court enhanced compensation to Rs. 7,000 per square foot of carpet area for affected flat owners and directed the Municipal Corporation to complete the demolition within a specified timeframe.

The Supreme Court examined whether the High Court was justified in directly adjudicating stamp duty liability on tripartite agreements involving the State, developer, and allottees. The Court held that such disputes must be referred to the competent authority under the Stamp Act and set aside the High Court's judgment, while directing the High Court to expeditiously dispose of the pending developer's writ petition.

The petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging provisions of the 2012 Amendment Act, while simultaneously maintaining a pending Article 226 petition before the High Court for identical relief. The Supreme Court held that invoking a constitutional remedy before the High Court precludes filing a parallel petition under Article 32 for the same facts, constituting an abuse of process. Consequently, the Article 32 petition was dismissed with costs of Rs. 1 lakh imposed on the petitioner.

The Supreme Court examined the scope of Order 18 Rule 17 and Section 151 of the CPC regarding the recall of witnesses after evidence has been closed. The Court held that this discretionary power must be exercised sparingly solely to clarify ambiguities, and cannot be invoked to fill omissions or lacunae in already led evidence, nor justified by a claim of 'no prejudice'. Consequently, the Court ruled that recalling a witness for further elaboration following suit consolidation is impermissible, thereby allowing the appeal and setting aside the lower courts' orders.

The Supreme Court reviewed its 2015 judgment concerning the publication of photographs of senior government functionaries in official advertisements. The Court modified the earlier order by extending permission to publish photographs of Governors and Chief Ministers, and allowing Departmental/Cabinet Ministers' photographs to be used in lieu of the Prime Minister or Chief Ministers. All other directives from the original judgment remain unchanged.

The appeal challenged the High Court's setting aside of a Charity Commissioner's sanction for the sale and re-development of a charitable trust property, centering on compliance with tenant consent requirements under Mumbai's Development Control Regulations. The Supreme Court restored the Trust's rights, holding that the mandatory 70% irrevocable written consent threshold was satisfied and that the original developer's enhanced monetary offer was fair and reasonable.

The Supreme Court examined whether a counter-claim could be filed after issues were framed but before evidence was concluded in a civil suit. Invoking Order VIII Rule 6A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the Court held that a counter-claim is legally permissible if the cause of action accrued before the defendant delivered their written statement. The Court allowed the appeals, reversing the High Court's order that had improperly rejected the counter-claim.

The appellant challenged the order of cognizance and summons in a Section 138 NI Act case, citing undue delay in filing the complaint, failure to examine the complainant under Section 200 CrPC, and omission of a jurisdictional enquiry under Section 202 CrPC. The Supreme Court held that Section 145 of the Negotiable Instruments Act permits affidavit evidence, thereby overriding the Section 200 CrPC requirement, but found the Magistrate failed to apply its mind to condone the filing delay or address territorial jurisdiction. Consequently, the appeals were allowed, and the Magistrate was directed to reconsider the delay and jurisdictional issues before passing fresh orders.

The Supreme Court examined whether a pre-deposit made before the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal under Section 18 of the SARFAESI Act constitutes a secured asset or debt. The Court held that the pre-deposit does not create any security interest in favor of the secured creditor and is therefore neither a secured asset nor a secured debt. Consequently, upon disposal or withdrawal of the appeal, the deposit must be refunded to the borrower, and the bank's claim of a lien under the Contract Act was rejected.

The Supreme Court upheld the convictions of accused A1 to A6 for murder and conspiracy under Sections 302 and 120B IPC, relying on cogent eyewitness testimony corroborated by medical evidence and valid Test Identification Parades. However, the Court set aside the conviction of A7 for unlawful assembly and abetment to murder, finding insufficient proof of his presence at the scene and his link to the conspiracy, particularly since the associated second group had been acquitted.

The Supreme Court held that a suit by a former minor to set aside a property transfer made by a guardian in violation of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, is governed by Article 60 of the Limitation Act, 1963, prescribing a three-year limitation from attaining majority. The Court ruled that Article 109, applicable to paternal alienation under Mitakshara law, does not apply to maternal or guardian transfers, and consequently dismissed the appeal.

The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and remitted the writ petition for fresh consideration. The core issue concerned the computation of the 3% reservation for differently abled persons under the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995. The Court held that such reservation must be calculated based on the total vacancies of the cadre, rather than the vacancies available in identified posts at the time of notification.

The Supreme Court held that a declaration regarding the validity of a marriage or matrimonial status falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of Family Courts under Sections 7 and 8 of the Family Courts Act, 1984, irrespective of whether the relief sought is affirmative or negative. The impugned High Court judgment was set aside and the matter was remitted for fresh consideration on merits.

The Supreme Court dismissed a criminal appeal challenging a maintenance order granted to a wife under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. The Court ruled that previously initiated but unsuccessful divorce proceedings do not terminate the marital relationship or render a domestic violence application inadmissible, upholding the wife's entitlement to maintenance.

The case concerns the rights of an alienee of Service-Inam land alienated between 1963 and 1978 after its re-grant to the original holder under the Karnataka Village Offices Act, 1961. The Court held that the re-granted title relates back to the Act's commencement, and under the doctrine of feeding the grant by estoppel, enures to the alienee's benefit, thereby validating their title. Consequently, the alienee cannot be evicted as an 'unauthorized holder,' and the Supreme Court allowed the appeals, restoring the lower courts' decrees.

The Supreme Court examined an appeal challenging a Consolidation Officer's order allotting land under Section 43A of the East Punjab Holdings Act, 1948. The Court found that the final order was passed without affording the appellant or proforma respondents a proper notice or hearing, rendering it procedurally defective. The matter was remitted back to the Consolidation Officer for fresh adjudication, with directions to strictly limit jurisdiction to correcting clerical or arithmetical errors and to examine the nature of possession and delay.

The appellants challenged the denial of statutory interest on enhanced compensation under Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, for the period during which reference proceedings were stayed at their instance. The Supreme Court held that such a stay is irrelevant to statutory entitlements and ruled that interest must be calculated from the date of dispossession to the date of payment, including the stay period. The appeals were allowed, directing the concerned authority to compute and deposit the dues.

The appellant sought allotment of 500 square yards of land each for himself and three family members under the Improvement Trust Rules following a second land acquisition, having already received 250 square yards for a prior acquisition. The Supreme Court held that each acquisition is independent, qualifying the family as local displaced persons for the second acquisition as well. However, exercising equity, the Court limited the allotment to 250 square yards each, partly allowing the appeals and directing the Trust to release the plots.

The Supreme Court clarified that a Magistrate's direction for investigation under Section 156(3) of the CrPC inherently requires the police to register an FIR before proceeding. The Court directed the concerned Magistrate and police to rectify their oversight by registering an appropriate FIR and to complete the investigation fairly within six months. The criminal appeal was allowed to this extent.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeals and remitted the matter to the Board of Revenue, holding that dismissing a pre-emption application solely because the statutory 10% deposit was made under a wrong treasury head amounts to an impermissibly pedantic approach. The Court ruled that substantive rights under land laws cannot be defeated on technical grounds when the deposit has indeed been made to the credit of the treasury, emphasizing that parties cannot be denied adjudication on merits due to inadvertent mistakes.

The Supreme Court held that Section 23 of the Travancore-Cochin High Court Act, 1125, which governs appeals when High Court judges differ, remains unaffected by Section 9 of the Kerala High Court Act, 1958. As a special law, it prevails over the general provision of Section 98(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure and applies uniformly to all appeals before the Kerala High Court.

The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order quashing criminal proceedings against association office bearers for alleged misappropriation of funds. The Court held that the allegations could not be treated as purely personal, particularly after investigation was complete and charges were framed, and noted that most charged offences were non-compoundable. Consequently, the complaint case was restored to the Chief Judicial Magistrate for trial.

The case examines whether a driving licence for light motor vehicles requires a specific endorsement to legally operate transport vehicles within the same weight class. Due to conflicting precedents and ambiguous statutory definitions regarding vehicle classifications, the Court referred the matter to a Larger Bench for a definitive ruling.

The Supreme Court examined whether a High Court can grant interim relief in a second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC without first admitting the appeal and formulating a substantial question of law. The Court held that formulating such a question is a mandatory precondition for admission, rendering the grant of an ex parte interim order procedurally invalid. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, affirming the High Court's correct decision to vacate the interim order.

The Supreme Court examined whether a development agreement between the DDA and a builder was frustrated under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act due to supervening environmental restrictions and Ridge management prohibitions. The Court ruled that the contract became impossible of performance because of intervening governmental clearances prohibiting construction, which neither party could have contemplated, and directed the DDA to refund the builder's deposited amount with 6% interest.

The Court examined whether sponsor logos ('On-Screen Credits') embedded in a live sports broadcast feed constitute commercial advertisements under the Sports Broadcasting Signals Act, 2007. It ruled that such logos are commercial advertisements and mandated that broadcasters must share the best available feed with Prasar Bharati completely free of them, or else share the advertising revenue. Dismissing the appeal, the Court emphasized the statute's purposive interpretation to ensure free-to-air access for the general public.

topics: Mandatory sharing of sports broadcast signals

query: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's conviction of the appellant under Sections 498A and 306 IPC for dowry-related cruelty and abetment to suicide, reversing the trial court's acquittal. The Court held that the delay in lodging the FIR was excusable given the victim's mother's mental state and the presence of infant children, and found that the presumption of suicide under Section 113A of the Evidence Act was rightly invoked due to unexplained injuries and the husband's failure to rebut it.

The Supreme Court examined whether a second appeal involving a dispute over land ownership and document interpretation involved a substantial question of law, which the High Court had dismissed as merely factual. The Court held that interpreting documents to determine title constitutes a substantial question of law, found a jurisdictional error in the High Court's dismissal, and allowed the appeal. The matter was remanded to the High Court to admit the appeal, frame appropriate substantial questions of law, and decide on merits after making statutory efforts for settlement.

topics: Ownership rights and title to land

query: The appellant challenged his conviction under Sections 304 Part II and 323 of the Indian Penal Code for causing death and simple injuries during a dispute. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the concurrent findings of the lower courts based on consistent eyewitness testimony were neither arbitrary nor perverse, thereby upholding the conviction.

The appellant challenged his conviction for possession of a commercial quantity of charas under the NDPS Act, alleging procedural defects during the search and the prosecution's failure to examine all cited witnesses. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, mandatory search safeguards under Sections 42, 43, and 50 were duly complied with, and the omission of one witness did not vitiate the trial given the conclusive remaining evidence. The Court also upheld the lower courts' refusal to consider the appellant's unsworn affidavit.

The Supreme Court dismissed the State of Haryana's criminal appeal against a High Court order acquitting the accused. The Court held that it would not interfere or re-appreciate evidence when the High Court's decision was based on cogent reasoning and fell within its jurisdiction, as there was no perversity or legal error in the lower court's findings.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal against a High Court order that quashed land acquisition notifications, finding that the invocation of the urgency clause was unjustified. However, due to substantial infrastructure development already undertaken on the acquired land, the Court declined to set aside the acquisition and instead awarded enhanced compensation of 64.7% and allotted developed abadi land to balance equities.

The appellant college was denied permanent affiliation for the 2015-16 academic session due to non-compliance with state-prescribed deadlines, yet admitted students without valid affiliation. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that administrative benefits cannot be extended beyond statutory time limits, but directed the University to process the affiliation application afresh. If affiliation is subsequently granted, the admitted students will be regularized for the next academic session covered by the new affiliation.

The Supreme Court examined whether a High Court's suo motu initiation of criminal contempt proceedings in 2015 for an article published in 2008 was barred by the one-year limitation period under Section 20 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. Holding that the initiation of proceedings commences at the time of filing the application or issuing notice, the Court ruled that the delayed action was time-barred and allowed the appeal.

The Supreme Court examined whether an application for rejection of an election petition under Order VII Rule 11 of the CPC must be disposed of before the trial commences. It held that the trial court is duty-bound to decide such applications before proceeding with the trial, setting aside the High Court's order for proceeding otherwise. On merits, the application for rejection was dismissed, but the appellant was granted an opportunity to file a written statement.

The Supreme Court held that a suit filed on January 3, 2011 was beyond the prescribed limitation period expiring on December 31, 2010, as the court registry was open on the intervening non-working Saturday of January 1, 2011. Relying on Sections 4 and 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the Court ruled that extension applies only when the court is closed during normal working hours, and Section 5 does not apply to civil suits. Consequently, the application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC was allowed and the recovery suit was dismissed.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, holding that under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the Chief Justice or his designate must prima facie determine the existence and validity of an arbitration agreement when disputed, rather than leaving it to the arbitrator. The impugned High Court order directing the arbitrator to decide the MoU's validity was set aside, and the matter was remitted to the High Court to adjudicate the issue on merits.

The Supreme Court held that tips collected from customers and distributed to hotel employees do not constitute 'salary' under the Income Tax Act, but are chargeable as 'income from other sources.' Consequently, Section 192 regarding Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on salary is not attracted, and employers acting merely as conduits for customer tips cannot be penalized for non-deduction.

topics: Income from Salary vs Other Sources

query: The Supreme Court examined whether the High Court correctly exonerated the insurance company from liability after finding the driver's driving licence invalid due to submission of a photocopy. The Court ruled in favour of the appellant, holding the insurer liable as the driver proved the licence in evidence without objection, the insurer failed to prove it was fake, and could not raise objections at a later stage, thereby allowing the appeals and directing compensation payment.

The Supreme Court allowed the civil appeal and restored the termination order of a part-time lecturer, overturning the High Court's reinstatement direction. The Court held that the appointment was temporary and for a fixed period under the Maharashtra Employees of Private Schools (Conditions of Service) Regulation Act, 1977, giving the respondent no right to claim permanent status or regularization.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appellant's appeal against conviction for forging loan applications and misappropriating government scheme funds. The Court upheld the High Court's finding that an Executive Magistrate could lawfully record handwriting specimens during the 1983-1986 investigation period, prior to the enactment of Section 311-A of the Cr.P.C., and affirmed the conviction based on corroborative oral and expert evidence. The Court declined to reduce the appellant's sentence despite his advanced age and health conditions, emphasizing the gravity of misusing public money.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's acquittal of a husband accused of murdering his wife, who died from severe burn injuries. Emphasizing that courts must scrutinize dying declarations for voluntariness and consistency rather than relying on them mechanically, the Court found the deceased's recorded statements naming an unknown stranger more credible than the father's oral account. Finding the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the appeal was dismissed.

The Supreme Court dismissed a writ petition under Article 32 seeking remission of sentence for petitioners convicted under the NDPS Act. The Court held that Article 32 cannot be invoked to grant remission as it is strictly limited to enforcing fundamental rights or addressing public interest litigation. It further clarified that constitutional remission powers under Articles 72 and 161 operate in a different domain than statutory remission under the CrPC, which is expressly barred by Section 32A of the NDPS Act.

The Supreme Court held that a landowner entering into a development agreement with a builder qualifies as a 'consumer' under Section 2(1)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, provided the arrangement is not a joint venture. Since the appellant was merely entitled to a specific share of constructed flats and did not participate in the construction business or assume commercial risks, the transaction did not fall under the commercial purpose exemption. The matter was remitted to the State Commission for fresh adjudication treating the appellant as a consumer.

The Supreme Court allowed a civil appeal concerning the rejection of a commercial tender bid for manpower services. It held that bidders must strictly adhere to essential tender conditions, including quoting fixed prices and complying with government-prescribed minimum wages, reversing the High Court's attempt to recalculate bids post-evaluation. The Court emphasized that writ jurisdiction cannot be utilized to forge a new bargain or alter established tender terms.

The Supreme Court dismissed a criminal appeal challenging the appellant's conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC. The Court held that the testimony of hostile witnesses remains legally reliable if unshaken during cross-examination and corroborated by other evidence, and reiterated its self-restrained jurisdiction under Article 136 not to interfere with concurrent factual findings of lower courts absent clear perversity.

The Court examined whether income derived from slot charter arrangements qualifies as relevant shipping income for the Tonnage Tax Scheme under Chapter XIIG of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and whether a valid net tonnage certificate is mandatory. It held that slot charter income falls under deemed tonnage, exempting the assessee from producing a physical certificate for such arrangements, and consequently dismissed the Revenue's appeals.

The Supreme Court examined whether delay in filing an objection against an arbitral award under Section 34(2) could be condoned by excluding time spent on a Section 11 application under Section 14 of the Limitation Act. The Court held that Section 14 is inapplicable as the proceedings do not relate to the same matter in issue and the respondent lacked requisite diligence and good faith. Consequently, the appeal was allowed and the High Court's order was set aside.

The appellant claimed Scheduled Caste status as a member of the Thandan community to secure a government school appointment, while the state argued she belonged to the Ezhava/Thiyya community, which was later excluded from the SC list. The Court held that the statutory amendment excluding these groups from SC status operates prospectively from 2007, and since the appellant was validly appointed in 1989 under the then-applicable order, she is entitled to continue enjoying the reservation benefits. The appeals are consequently allowed.

The Supreme Court set aside the conviction under Section 302 IPC, holding that the trial court violated mandatory procedural safeguards under Sections 216 and 217 of the CrPC when it altered the charge from abetment of suicide to murder at a late stage. The Court ruled that such alteration necessitated recalling witnesses and permitting cross-examination, and the failure to do so vitiated the trial, resulting in the sentence being reduced to the period already undergone.

The Supreme Court held that the period during which an interim stay on assessment proceedings or an integral step like a special audit is in operation must be excluded while computing the two-year limitation period for completing a block assessment under the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Court further ruled that the limitation period should be counted from the date the search operation was finally concluded. Consequently, the civil appeal was dismissed.

The Supreme Court examined the legality of government memoranda denying statutory 3% reservation for persons with disabilities (PWD) in identified Group A and B posts, particularly those filled through promotion. Holding the memoranda illegal and inconsistent with the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995, the Court ruled that once a post is identified as suitable for PWD, the mandatory reservation must be applied irrespective of the recruitment mode, clarifying that the Indra Sawhney restriction on promotional reservation does not apply to PWD.

The Supreme Court examined whether the limitation period for a recovery suit against a defaulting hirer under a hire-purchase agreement runs from the first default or the subsequent sale of the vehicle. The Court held that the right to sue accrued on the date of the initial default, which constituted a breach of contract, and thus the suit filed beyond three years was barred by limitation under Articles 55 and 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963. The civil appeal was consequently dismissed.

The Supreme Court upheld the conviction and life imprisonment for appellant Mumtaz, ruling that a reliable dying declaration corroborated by circumstantial evidence is sufficient for conviction despite inconsistencies with eyewitness accounts. The Court set aside the life sentence for appellant Dilshad, recognizing him as a juvenile under the 2000 Act on the date of the offense, and remitted his matter to the Jurisdictional Juvenile Justice Board for appropriate disposal.

The Supreme Court examined whether registered Private Tour Operators (PTOs) for Haj must annually furnish documentary proof of past operations for quota allotment under the approved government policy. The Court held that the evidentiary stipulation applies only to initial registration for category classification, and once registered, a PTO's status remains valid until 2017 unless deregistered for valid reasons. The Government was directed to consider all eligible PTOs for the 2016 Haj quota allotment in strict accordance with the approved scheme.

The Supreme Court held that criminal proceedings and property attachment under the Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance, 1944 cannot continue against a deceased accused, as prosecution abates upon death. The lower courts committed a gross error by treating a dead accused as guilty and attaching his property, violating foundational criminal jurisprudence and the presumption of innocence. The appeal was allowed, setting aside the impugned attachment orders.

The Supreme Court allowed the petitioner's application for the appointment of a sole arbitrator under Sections 11(5) and 11(9) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The Court held that because a valid arbitration clause governs the Buyers Agreement, all disputes regarding unpaid invoices and alleged contractual breaches must be referred to arbitration. A former Delhi High Court judge was appointed to adjudicate the commercial disputes, leaving the parties to present their claims and counterclaims before the tribunal.

This case concerns the extradition of a French national accused of conspiracy in the assassination of a Chilean Senator to Chile. The Supreme Court held that the Extradition Act, 1962 applies to Chile based on a binding 1897 treaty and the principle of reciprocity, and that a requisition by a foreign embassy is legally valid. The Court dismissed the writ petition, ruling that the applicability of the Extradition Act to foreign states is a political executive decision outside the scope of judicial review, and remitted the matter to the magistrate for a merits-based decision on extradition.

The Supreme Court allowed a civil appeal against a High Court order that prematurely appointed an arbitrator under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The Court held that the respondent contractor failed to wait for the contractually stipulated 60 days for the Railways to submit a panel of names, rendering the application premature and preserving the Railways' right to appoint arbitrators as per the agreement.

The appeal examines whether a second complaint to the District Forum under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is maintainable when the first complaint was dismissed for default or non-prosecution. The Court held that since the Consumer Protection Rules lack a provision analogous to Order IX Rule 9(1) of the CPC, a second complaint is permissible provided it explains the earlier default. Consequently, the appeal is allowed and the matter is remitted to the National Commission for adjudication on merits.

The Supreme Court dismissed the petitioner's transfer petitions seeking to move quashing petitions from the Kerala High Court to Delhi, holding that the pending investigation and constitution of a special state police team make the Kerala High Court better positioned to monitor the case. The Court declined to direct a CBI investigation, reiterating that such extraordinary powers must be exercised rarely in exceptional circumstances, but instead directed the Kerala DGP to constitute a special investigation team to ensure a fair inquiry.

The Supreme Court held that electronic survey instruments fall under Entry 14 of Part F of the Tamil Nadu General Sales Tax Act, 1959, attracting a 16% tax rate instead of 3% under Entry 50 of Part B. Recognizing the appellant's bona fide belief stemming from statutory amendments and the absence of mens rea, the Court set aside the balance penalty while refusing a refund of amounts already paid.

The Supreme Court dismissed criminal appeals challenging convictions under Sections 302 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code for murder. The Court upheld the lower courts' findings, holding that the deceased's father's ocular testimony was corroborated by medical evidence, the delay in lodging the FIR was satisfactorily explained, and the prosecution's case contained no inherent improbabilities warranting interference.

The appellants challenged the High Court's enhancement of their sentence to five years rigorous imprisonment for offences under Sections 325/149 IPC, claiming parity with three co-accused granted probation due to extreme old age. The Supreme Court held the parity claim misconceived, noting that since the victim could not depose and no specific role in causing the head injury could be assigned to any convict, the enhanced sentence was unjustified. Accordingly, the Court reduced the sentence back to three years rigorous imprisonment while maintaining the convictions and sentences for other minor offences.

The Supreme Court upheld the Commissioner of Income Tax’s suo motu revisional powers under Section 263 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, ruling that jurisdiction arises when an order is erroneous and prejudicial to revenue, provided the assessee receives a fair opportunity of hearing. The Court clarified that a show cause notice is not mandatory under Section 263, set aside the conflicting Tribunal and High Court orders, and restored the C.I.T.’s revisional order.

The Supreme Court allowed a criminal appeal, acquitting appellants convicted for causing injuries and death in a village clash. The Court held that when the prosecution suppresses the origin of the incident and fails to explain injuries sustained by the accused, including fatal injuries to their father, the benefit of doubt and right to private defence must be granted, overturning the High Court's free fight conviction.

The State of Madhya Pradesh challenged a High Court order directing it to accept late-delivered printed booklets from a contractor after the contract had been cancelled due to time expiry. The Supreme Court held that time was the essence of the contract, and the automatic cancellation upon expiry of the extended deadline meant the printers had no right to supply or claim payment for work done thereafter. The Court set aside the High Court's judgment, allowing the appeal and directing payment only for booklets supplied within the stipulated extended period.

The Supreme Court upheld the validity of the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) for MBBS/BDS admissions, ruling that it does not violate State rights or the autonomy of private and minority institutions. The Court clarified that NEET merely sets eligibility standards under Union legislative competence, while States retain concurrent power for implementation. To alleviate student hardship, the Court directed a second examination (NEET-II) for eligible candidates who missed or were unsatisfied with NEET-I, modifying its earlier orders accordingly.

topics: Autonomy of Private and Minority Institutions

query: The petition sought a writ mandamus directing the respondents to conduct the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) for medical admissions for the 2016-17 academic session. The Court accepted the respondents' assurance to hold NEET pursuant to the 2010 MCI/DCI notifications, clarified that this order operates notwithstanding any prior judicial orders against holding NEET, and noted that pending related petitions would remain unaffected.

The Supreme Court upheld the disqualification of GYT-TPL JV's bid for the Nagpur Metro viaduct project, ruling that the tender issuer is best positioned to interpret its own tender conditions. The Court emphasized that judicial interference in administrative decisions is only permissible if the decision is perverse, arbitrary, or mala fide, rather than merely reflecting a differing interpretation of the tender terms.

The appellant was convicted for kidnapping, murder, and attempted rape of a seven-year-old girl, and sentenced to death. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction based on a complete chain of circumstantial evidence but modified the conviction to rape, relying on medical findings. Finding the case did not warrant the 'rarest of rare' criteria for capital punishment, the Court commuted the sentence to life imprisonment, directing that the appellant shall not be released until he completes 25 years of actual imprisonment.

The Supreme Court allowed the criminal appeal, quashing the convictions of three female appellants under Sections 307/149 and 148 of the IPC for an alleged assault arising from a land dispute. The Court found that the lower courts erred by uncritically accepting the victim's contradictory and improved testimony, which lacked medical corroboration and independent witness support. Consequently, the appellants were acquitted on the benefit of doubt.

The Supreme Court disposed of an interlocutory application seeking that postgraduate medical admissions for the 2016-17 academic year be based solely on a common entrance test. The Court rejected the plea to extend examination deadlines, noting it would violate the statutory timeline under the Post-Graduate Medical Education Regulations, 2000 and compromise transparency. Instead, it directed private colleges to admit students based on inter-se merit from the already-conducted All India Examination results, with counseling and fee collection managed by the State.

The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Madhya Pradesh Private Medical and Dental Post Graduate Courses Entrance Examination Rules, 2009 and the related 2007 State Act, which regulated admissions, fees, and reservations in private unaided colleges. The Court ruled that regulatory measures like common entrance tests and fee oversight are reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6), satisfy the doctrine of proportionality, and fall within the State's legislative competence, without violating the fundamental rights of private educational institutions.

The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, holding that the doctrine of promissory estoppel applies to compel the Kerala Government to exempt the appellant from building tax for the period Section 3A of the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975 was in force. Relief was denied for the post-1993 period when the section was omitted, as estoppel must yield when its application contravenes statute. The Court ruled that the government's failure to issue the exemption notification during the statutory period was arbitrary and vitiated by non-application of mind.

The case concerns the Revenue's statutory liability to pay interest on a delayed refund of central excise duty to an assessee. The Supreme Court held that the adjudicatory process for a refund application must be concluded within three months, and the obligation to pay interest under Section 11-BB commences immediately upon the expiry of this period from the date of receiving the application. Consequently, the Court affirmed the assessee's entitlement to interest for the delay in processing the refund.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appellants' special appeals against the High Court's dismissal of their writ and review petitions concerning land grabbing proceedings. The Court upheld the lower forums' findings that the respondents' title was firmly established and rejected the appellants' claims due to their failure to lead evidence on title and possession. Additionally, the plea of procedural non-compliance was dismissed as unsustainable, given the appellants' prior awareness of the proceedings, deliberate suppression of facts, and belated raising of the issue, which barred them under the clean hands doctrine.

The Supreme Court upheld the Tribunal's finding that the transfer of iron ore pellets between sister companies under a joint procurement policy constituted a transfer, not a sale. Consequently, the valuation for CENVAT credit reversal must be based on the original supplier's invoice, and post-manufacturing expenses cannot be added as additional consideration. The Revenue's appeals were dismissed.

The case examined whether a provisional appointment to a post reserved for Scheduled Tribes becomes final and protected from termination after the applicant's caste claim is subsequently found invalid. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the appointment was explicitly provisional and subject to verification, and since it had not attained confirmation or finality before the termination order was issued, the department was lawfully entitled to terminate the appellant's service.

The appellant sought to amend a dismissed Form 7 application for occupancy rights to claim a different parcel of land after the statutory cut-off date had passed. The Supreme Court held that such amendment was impermissible as it amounted to a fresh claim circumventing the Act's deadline, and the Tribunal could only correct clerical or arithmetical errors after finality. The appeal was accordingly dismissed.

The Supreme Court examined whether a commission agent displaced from a de-notified market has a legal right to be allotted a shop at Gazipur Mandi. The Court held that the respondent had no absolute legal right to a shop under the prevailing policy, but his long-pending claim warranted consideration alongside other eligible applicants for any surplus shops, subject to availability. Additionally, a 2014 notification exempted him from needing a license to continue his business at his current location.

The appellant was convicted for murdering her husband based on circumstantial evidence and an extra-judicial confession made to the deceased's sister. The Supreme Court acquitted her, ruling that the prosecution failed to complete the chain of circumstances beyond a reasonable doubt, the uncorroborated confession to an inimical witness inspired no confidence, and the recovered items were not linked to the offence.

The Supreme Court held that Article 233(2) of the Constitution prohibits only the appointment of persons already in state or union service as District Judges, but does not bar their participation in the selection process. Compelling serving subordinate judicial officers to resign merely to appear in selection interviews violates their fundamental rights under Articles 14 and 16. The Court directed the respondents to permit the appellants to participate in the selection process without insisting on prior resignation.

topics: Right to Participate in Selection Process

query: The Supreme Court dismissed the criminal appeal, upholding the conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC based on the victim's oral statement and the first dying declaration recorded by an Executive Magistrate. The Court ruled that when multiple dying declarations exist, each must be independently evaluated on its own merit, and the third declaration alleging accidental death was rightly rejected due to procedural defects, lack of thumb impression, and factual inconsistencies.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that appointments to Fast Track Courts are ad hoc in nature and do not confer rights for regular promotion or seniority over direct recruits appointed to substantive posts. The Court clarified that beneficiaries of ad hoc promotional schemes cannot claim parity with permanent cadre recruits, thereby upholding the High Court's seniority list.

The Supreme Court examined the validity of an environmental clearance granted for iron ore mining expansion and the Ministry of Environment and Forests' subsequent order deleting the initial two-year validity period. The Court held that the deletion order was cryptic and failed to adhere to mandatory environmental protection procedures, including public hearings and state-level authority scrutiny. Consequently, the Ministry was directed to reassess the clearance by strictly following statutory requirements before deciding on its continuation.

The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of criminal defamation provisions under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 199 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court ruled that criminal defamation constitutes a reasonable restriction on freedom of speech under Article 19(2), balancing it with the fundamental right to reputation under Article 21, and held that the term 'defamation' carries an independent constitutional meaning not constrained by the noscitur a sociis rule.

The Supreme Court held that Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 prohibits the withdrawal of land acquisition proceedings once possession has been lawfully taken from the landowners. Consequently, the Court quashed the High Court's judgment that had invalidated the acquisition, ruling that the Government's repeated attempts to withdraw the acquisition after taking possession were legally unsustainable. The civil appeals were allowed, affirming the validity of the original acquisition proceedings.

The Supreme Court held that the Income Tax Department had the right to recover outstanding tax dues once the company's net worth turned positive and its rehabilitation scheme under the Sick Industrial Companies Act expired. The Court deferred the question of waiving interest and penalty to the BIFR for clarification, while permitting the Revenue to attach and sell company properties to recover principal dues.

The petitioner challenged the validity of the 1997 Rules permitting former Chief Ministers of Uttar Pradesh to occupy government bungalows for life, arguing they contravened the 1981 Act which limits such retention to 15 days. The Supreme Court held that the 1997 Rules are merely executive instructions that cannot override statutory provisions, and their life-tenure allotment violates Article 14 of the Constitution. Consequently, the Court struck down the Rules, directed former Chief Ministers and their families to vacate the bungalows within two months, and ordered the cancellation of unlawful allotments to private trusts.

The Supreme Court allowed the civil appeal, ruling that Section 492(3) of the Kerala Municipality Act, 1994 requires a landlord's written consent only for initial licence applications, not for renewals. The Court held that a valid statutory tenancy implies landlord authority for legitimate business use, and tenants cannot be deprived of conducting lawful business merely due to withheld consent.

The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Rules 3 and 3A of the Allahabad High Court Rules, 1952, which require advocates not enrolled in the state Bar Council to appear alongside a local advocate. The Court held that these rules are regulatory rather than prohibitive, serve the public interest by ensuring accountability and smooth court functioning, and constitute reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

The appellant challenged the rejection of his claim for statutory interest under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, after voluntarily accepting a consent award under state rules without protest. The Supreme Court held that by entering into an agreement and accepting the consolidated compensation without demur, the appellant lost the remedy of seeking enhancement under Section 18, thereby extinguishing the substantive cause of action for statutory interest.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, holding that a renewal of a mining lease stands on the same footing as a fresh grant. Consequently, the State Government was empowered to impose conditions, such as establishing a captive plant, on lease renewals, provided prior permission for de-reservation and condition imposition had been granted by the Central Government.

topics: Imposition of conditions on mineral concessions

query: The Supreme Court dismissed a Special Leave Petition filed by a defendant who repeatedly sought adjournments on frivolous grounds, causing severe delay and hardship to an elderly plaintiff. The Court condemned such dilatory tactics as a clear abuse of process, imposed substantial costs, and foreclosed the defendant's right to cross-examine witnesses, emphasizing the institutional responsibility of counsels and the imperative of speedy civil litigation.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order directing the State to accept the sole responsive bidder for a dam construction project. The Court held that the government retains the prerogative to cancel a tender, particularly when there is a lack of adequate competition, and that the tender committee's decision was reasonable and not arbitrary. Judicial review in such matters is strictly limited to checking for mala fide, unreasonableness, or arbitrariness in the decision-making process.

topics: Right to Cancel or Refuse Tender

query: The Supreme Court upheld SEBI's findings that respondents illegally cornered shares meant for retail investors in IPOs through hundreds of benami and fictitious demat accounts, engaging in fraudulent off-market transactions. Allowing SEBI's appeals, the Court quashed the Securities Appellate Tribunal's order, ruling that such irregularities violated the SEBI Act, SCRA, and applicable regulations, thereby harming small investors and market integrity.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's conviction of an advocate for contempt but set aside the imprisonment sentence due to his advanced age. Exercising appellate jurisdiction due to prolonged inaction by the Bar Councils, the Court suspended the appellant's enrollment for two years under Section 24A of the Advocates Act and imposed an additional five-year suspension for professional misconduct. The appellant remains debarred from appearing in Etah district courts until he purges himself of contempt.

The Supreme Court examined whether employees could withdraw their Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) applications after the scheme's validity period had expired. Holding that a VRS scheme is contractual in nature, the Court ruled that while an employee may withdraw their offer during the scheme's validity period, withdrawal after its closure is not permissible. Accordingly, the High Court's order reinstating employees who withdrew post-closure was set aside.

The appeal concerns whether former government employees transferred to a road transport corporation are entitled to pensionary benefits introduced decades after their retirement, having previously availed only provident fund benefits. The Supreme Court held that by accepting the departmental merger, continuing service, and retiring with CPF benefits without protest, the respondents acquiesced to the change and cannot later challenge their entitlement to pension. Consequently, the claim for retrospective pensionary benefits was dismissed as untenable.

The Supreme Court held that packing materials for tea cannot be classified as raw materials, components, or inputs under the Karnataka Tax on Entry of Goods Act, 1979, to claim tax exemptions or reduced rates. Since packing materials are separately categorized in the Act's schedule, the appellant's claim was rejected and the civil appeal was dismissed.

The Supreme Court examined the limited jurisdiction of a Joint Labour Commissioner under Section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, regarding the dismissal of a bus driver for causing a fatal accident. The Court held that the Commissioner exceeded his jurisdiction by reappreciating evidence and substituting his own judgment for that of the disciplinary authority, noting that adequate material was on record and the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur applied. Accordingly, the approval for dismissal was granted, reversing the High Court's decision.

The appellant, a physically handicapped candidate selected in the 2001 state service examination, sought appointment as a Deputy Collector under a backlog quota after initially being appointed as a Trade Tax Officer. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's denial of relief, ruling that retrospective adjustment would unduly disturb the seniority of candidates appointed in intervening years. The civil appeal was accordingly dismissed.

The Supreme Court held that the availability of a criminal revision under Section 397 Cr.P.C. does not bar the High Court from exercising its inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to prevent abuse of process or secure ends of justice. Accordingly, the Court allowed the appeals and remitted the matters back to the High Court for fresh consideration on merits.

The Supreme Court allowed criminal appeals filed by Standard Chartered Bank, setting aside a High Court order that had quashed summons against the Executive Director and whole-time Directors of a company for dishonouring cheques. The Court held that Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 creates constructive liability for persons in charge of and responsible for the day-to-day conduct of the company's business at the time of the offence, and ruled that the High Court erred by failing to properly scrutinize the complaint's specific assertions regarding their roles.

The Supreme Court held that a valid nomination under Section 79 of the West Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1983, is binding on the co-operative society, which is mandated to transfer the deceased member's share to the nominated person. The Court clarified that this administrative transfer does not extinguish the legal heirs' rights, who may separately pursue succession or inheritance claims in a competent court.

The appellant challenged a Central Government policy that unilaterally revised the price of Regasified Liquefied Natural Gas (RLNG) under long-term supply contracts, alleging a violation of vested contractual rights and equality. The Supreme Court upheld the policy, ruling that the executive possesses constitutional competence under Article 73 to regulate essential commodities and that courts must exercise restraint over commercial policy decisions unless they are arbitrary, unreasonable, or mala fide. Finding that the policy applied uniformly to all long-term RLNG consumers without discrimination, the Court held it did not violate Article 14 and dismissed the appeal.

The Supreme Court examined whether Visvesvaraya Technological University qualifies for tax exemption under Section 10(23C)(iiab) of the Income Tax Act, which mandates that the institution be solely educational and substantially government-financed. The Court held that while the university satisfies the non-profit educational purpose requirement, it fails the financing condition as direct government grants constituted less than 5% of total receipts and statutory fee collections do not qualify as government funding. Consequently, the appeals were dismissed and the claimed tax exemption was denied.

The case examines whether a candidate born to Muslim parents who later converted to Sikhism retains his Scheduled Caste status to contest a reserved constituency.
